prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit.

We represent: defendant officer.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that an officer's use of a taser on an actively resisting suspect does not violate clearly established Fourth Amendment law.

Cite at least six decisions of the Sixth Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.
answer:
## ARGUMENT

### I. Officer [Name] is entitled to qualified immunity because tasing an actively resisting suspect does not violate clearly established Fourth Amendment law.

Qualified immunity shields officers from civil liability unless (1) they violated a constitutional right that (2) was "clearly established" at the time of the conduct. *Pearson v. Callahan*, 555 U.S. 223, 232 (2009). A right is clearly established only if existing precedent places the constitutional question "beyond debate," *Ashcroft v. al-Kidd*, 563 U.S. 731, 741 (2011), and the Supreme Court has repeatedly cautioned courts not to define clearly established law "at a high level of generality." *Id.* at 742. In the excessive-force context, where the inquiry is fact-bound, plaintiffs must identify precedent that "squarely governs" the specific circumstances the officer confronted. *Mullenix v. Luna*, 577 U.S. 7, 13-14 (2015) (per curiam); *see also White v. Pauly*, 580 U.S. 73, 79 (2017) (per curiam). Plaintiff cannot make that showing.

**A. The force was objectively reasonable under *Graham*.**

Excessive-force claims turn on the objective reasonableness of the force in light of the severity of the crime, the immediate threat posed by the suspect, and whether he was actively resisting or attempting to flee. *Graham v. Connor*, 490 U.S. 386, 396 (1989). This Court applies those factors from the perspective of a reasonable officer on the scene, not with hindsight. *Pollard v. City of Columbus*, 780 F.3d 395, 402 (6th Cir. 2015).

Active resistance weighs heavily in the officer's favor. This Court has repeatedly held that officers may use a taser to gain control of a suspect who refuses commands and physically resists arrest. In *Hagans v. Franklin County Sheriff's Office*, 695 F.3d 505, 509-11 (6th Cir. 2012), the Court granted qualified immunity where an officer used a taser on a suspect who resisted efforts to take him into custody. In *Rudlaff v. Gillispie*, 791 F.3d 638, 641-43 (6th Cir. 2015), the Court likewise held that officers who used a taser against a suspect who was resisting and had not been brought under control did not violate the Fourth Amendment. And in *Coble v. City of White House*, 634 F.3d 865, 870-71 (6th Cir. 2011), the Court found no clearly established violation where officers used a taser against a suspect who refused to comply with their efforts to arrest him. Here, as in those cases, [Plaintiff] [describe resistance: pulled away, refused to place hands behind his back, struck or struggled with officers] after being given clear commands. A taser deployment was a measured, less-lethal response to that resistance.

**B. No clearly established law put Officer [Name] on notice that the force was unlawful.**

The decisions in which this Court has denied immunity involve a materially different fact pattern: suspects who were not resisting, had been subdued, or were already restrained. *See Goodwin v. City of Painesville*, 781 F.3d 314, 326-28 (6th Cir. 2015) (right to be free from tasing is clearly established when a suspect is not actively resisting or has stopped resisting); *Roell v. Hamilton County*, 870 F.3d 471, 480-83 (6th Cir. 2017) (denying immunity where the suspect was subdued and not resisting when force was applied). The rule that emerges from these cases is that the gratuitous use of a taser on a compliant or incapacitated person is unlawful. The corollary is that an officer who tases a person who is actively resisting acts within the bounds of clearly established law. *Hagans*, 695 F.3d at 509-11; *Rudlaff*, 791 F.3d at 641-43.

This line of authority defeats Plaintiff's claim. Plaintiff cannot cite a decision of the Supreme Court or this Court holding that tasing a suspect who was actively resisting violates the Fourth Amendment. Without such a case, a reasonable officer in Officer [Name]'s position could have believed the taser use was lawful, and that is all qualified immunity requires. *See Mullenix*, 577 U.S. at 12; *Mullins v. Cyranek*, 805 F.3d 760, 765-67 (6th Cir. 2015).

**C. Plaintiff's attempt to characterize the encounter as one of compliance fails.**

To the extent Plaintiff argues that resistance had ceased before the taser was deployed, the question is what a reasonable officer would have perceived in the seconds before force was used, not what a later review of the events might suggest. *Graham*, 490 U.S. at 396-97. Officers are not required to gamble that a resisting suspect has abruptly decided to submit. Because the record shows that [Plaintiff] was still resisting when the taser was deployed, *Goodwin* and *Roell* do not apply, and *Hagans*, *Rudlaff*, and *Coble* control.

### Conclusion

Officer [Name]'s use of a taser on an actively resisting suspect was objectively reasonable and did not violate clearly established law. This Court should hold that Officer [Name] is entitled to qualified immunity.
